text: It's 11.47 at night.
A mother and her daughter are standing by a window.
Outside, the moon is shining above the ocean.
Then, without warning, it disappears.
The little girl points at the sky.
Mom, where did it go?
Her mother has no answer.
Within minutes, videos begin spreading across the internet.
People gather in the streets.
News channels interrupt their broadcasts.
Astronomers turn their telescopes toward an empty patch of sky.
The moon hasn't exploded.
It hasn't moved behind another planet.
It's simply gone.
And for the first time in human history,
Earth has no moon.
But here's what nobody realizes yet.
The disappearance itself isn't necessarily what would cause the greatest damage.
The consequences could begin unfolding in the oceans,
among animals that depend on the moon to survive and reproduce.

the world hasn't ended.

The oceans.

the moon has exerted gravitational forces that help create the tides.
Twice a day in many places,
the sea rises and falls.

But now, the moon's contribution is gone.

that change could create a remarkable problem.

thousands of tiny fish eggs are waiting.

adult grunion actually swim out of the ocean and onto the beach.

The eggs remain hidden underground.

another series of high tides normally reaches them.

the remaining tides might not reach the places where eggs have been buried.

entire local populations could struggle.

and the system that once worked so precisely may begin failing.
But the consequences wouldn't stop at a California beach.
Far away,
beneath the warm waters of tropical oceans,
scientists could encounter an even more extraordinary problem.
Coral reefs.
They're among the most diverse ecosystems on Earth.
And although they may look like underwater plants or rocks,
corals are living animals.
Some reproduce through remarkable synchronized spawning events.
On certain nights,
thousands of coral colonies release reproductive cells into the ocean.

Timing is critical.
If the cells are released too far apart,
the chances of successful reproduction can decrease.
So how do corals coordinate these enormous events?
For some species,
changes in moonlight provide important signals.

The expected spawning season arrives.
The usual lunar light signals never do.
Some corals might still respond to temperature,
seasonal changes, or other environmental cues.
Others could struggle to synchronize their reproductive timing.
Instead of releasing their cells together,
spawning could become scattered across different nights.
And in some places,
that could mean fewer successfully fertilized eggs,
fewer larvae,
and fewer new coral colonies growing into the next generation.
The reef wouldn't necessarily die overnight,
but imagine this disruption happening repeatedly,
year after year.
Coral populations already facing pollution,
warming oceans, and other pressures
could become less capable of recovering from damage.
And when coral reefs struggle,
the consequences can spread through the ecosystem.
Because reefs aren't simply beautiful underwater landscapes,
they provide shelter, feeding grounds, and nursery habitats
for extraordinary numbers of fish and other marine creatures.
A damaged reef can mean fewer suitable places for young fish to survive.

There is another role the moon has played over billions of years.

Earth's rotational behavior could evolve differently over very long periods.

potentially changing the character of seasons and influencing climate patterns.
